issues.description: The procedure section explicitly states that the individual memory test uses open-ended questions, and the opening of the analysis plan confirms this as a deliberate methodological departure from prior work. However, later in the same analysis plan section the authors write that 'the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format,' directly contradicting the stated design. These two formats have fundamentally different psychometric properties, scoring procedures, response bias profiles, and comparability to prior MORI-technique studies. The contradiction makes it impossible to evaluate the study's measurement approach, and means one section of the manuscript must be incorrect.
issues.quote: Procedure (Section 2.5): 'The test will contain 20 open-ended questions, eight of which will cover all the critical details.' Analysis plan (Section 3): 'First we will examine the memory conformity effect...but with modification concerning applying open-ended questions.' Then later in Section 3: 'In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.'

issues.description: The manuscript contains a direct self-contradiction about when the interventions are administered. In one passage of the introduction the authors explicitly state they chose to place the warning after the collaborative recall. In a later passage of the same introduction they state the opposite—that interventions are placed before collaborative recall—and give a rationale for this. The actual procedure described in Section 2.5 lists the phase order as: (1) movie, (2) collaborative recall, (3) intervention, (4) individual memory test, placing interventions after collaborative recall. This means the theoretical rationale offered for pre-exposure inoculation ('we wanted to inoculate participants against the influence of misinformation before it could take effect') does not match the actual procedure, undermining the theoretical framing of the study.
issues.quote: 'In the present study we decided to place the warning after the collaborative recall (see the rationale for the research below).' Versus: 'What is important, we decided to place the methods inducing resistance to misinformation before the collaborative recall phase (that is, before exposing participants to misinformation).' Versus procedure: '(1) presenting the original material, (2) collaborative recall (including misinformation), (3) three procedures to reduce vulnerability to misinformation...and (4) an individual memory test.'

issues.description: The fundamental unit of data collection is the dyad: participants interact with a specific partner, exchange misinformation, and are mutually influenced. Despite this, the analysis plan uses a standard two-factor ANOVA that treats individual participants as the unit of analysis and assumes independence of observations. Members of each pair share a discussion, are exposed to each other's specific errors and response styles, and potentially reinforce each other's memory distortions. This violates the independence assumption of ANOVA, inflates the effective degrees of freedom, and will produce anti-conservative (too-small) standard errors and p-values. The appropriate approach would be to model the dyad as the unit of randomization, use multilevel modeling accounting for pair-level clustering, or at minimum report and correct for intraclass correlation within pairs. This issue is particularly acute because the interaction effect—the key test of intervention efficacy—is also susceptible to this inflation.
issues.quote: 'The results will be analyzed by means of a two-factor ANOVA, with one within-subjects factor with two levels (discussed vs. non-discussed items) and one between-subjects factor with four levels (three groups of methods of reducing memory conformity and the control group).'

issues.description: The analysis plan describes two mutually contradictory rules for classifying discussed items. First, the authors establish a nuanced rule: if a partner happens to provide an answer consistent with what the participant saw (e.g., correctly guessing 'white mug'), the discussion item will NOT be classified as containing misinformation. This is methodologically sensible. However, immediately after, a blanket rule is stated: 'we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner's differing version.' These two rules are logically incompatible. The blanket categorization would inflate apparent misinformation exposure and misclassify some control-condition-like trials as misinformation trials, biasing the primary within-subjects comparison.
issues.quote: 'However, if the partner provided an answer consistent with what the participant had seen, that is, "white mug"...the situation will not be classified as misleading.' Versus: 'In addition, while scoring the individual memory test accuracy on the discussed questions (items containing misleading information), we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation.'

issues.description: The Extended Warning and Education about Memory conditions each involve listening to a single approximately 7-minute podcast. The Demonstration and Motivation condition, however, involves substantially more activity: listening to experimenter-read DRM word lists, completing a written recall sheet, receiving detailed feedback on false memories (including checking for specific lure words and receiving an explanation), and then also listening to a motivational podcast. This means participants in the Demonstration and Motivation condition spend considerably more total time on intervention-related material than participants in the other conditions. Any observed difference in efficacy between conditions could therefore be confounded with total exposure time and amount of processing rather than the specific content of each intervention. The control condition timing is also unspecified.
issues.quote: 'First, in order to demonstrate to participants that they are vulnerable to influence, a substantially shortened and simplified procedure based on the DRM paradigm will be used...Next, the participants' motivation to resist memory suggestibility will consist in them listening to a podcast with information that inaccurate testimony are the main causes of erroneous court judgments.' Versus: 'The extended warning will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast' and 'The training will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast.'

issues.description: The theoretical framework and the rationale for all three interventions depend critically on participants being 'aware of discrepancies' between what they saw in the movie and what their partner said. The authors state explicitly: 'our methods are expected to be effective in terms of informational influence...This, naturally, relates only to participants who are aware of the inconsistencies.' They further predict: 'effectiveness of our methods will be higher among people aware of discrepancies between the original information and misinformation than among those unaware.' Despite this being the core moderator hypothesis, no procedure for measuring discrepancy awareness is described anywhere in the methods or analysis plan. Without measuring this variable, the key mechanistic hypothesis cannot be tested, and null results on the primary outcomes cannot be interpreted (e.g., it would be impossible to distinguish 'intervention failed for aware participants' from 'no participants were aware of discrepancies').
issues.quote: 'Thus, we expect that effectiveness of our methods will be higher among people aware of discrepancies between the original information and misinformation than among those unaware of such discrepancies.' / 'From the above reasoning it follows that our methods of reducing the memory conformity effect are directed towards the participants who are aware of the discrepancy between both the original information and the misinformation obtained from the partner.'

issues.description: The authors conclude that normative social influence is 'completely ruled out' because the individual memory test involves no interpersonal pressure. This reasoning conflates the moment of influence with the moment of expression. Normative influence during the discussion phase could cause participants to publicly agree with their partner, and this public compliance could then produce memory updating (source monitoring confusion about whether the partner's version is now their own recollection), which is then expressed in the individual test. Ruling out normative influence at the test stage does not rule out normative influence at the encoding/discussion stage. This premature dismissal is consequential because the interventions are then theorized exclusively around informational influence mechanisms, potentially missing an important process the interventions could also target or be undermined by.
issues.quote: 'Given the fact that the individual memory test does not include any element of direct interpersonal pressure, we assumed that the normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect is completely ruled out in this study: participants work on their own and do not compare their answers with anybody, therefore there is no cost of disagreeing.'

issues.subcategory: DRM does not measure the target construct
issues.description: The Demonstration and Motivation condition uses the DRM paradigm to demonstrate to participants that their memory is fallible. However, the DRM measures susceptibility to associative semantic false memories—words strongly associated with an unstudied critical lure are falsely recalled—which is a fundamentally different cognitive mechanism from the social conformity process being studied in the MORI paradigm, where witnesses adopt another person's specific, verbally communicated, version of an event. The theoretical gap between these two phenomena is substantial: DRM errors arise from spreading activation and implicit associative responses, while memory conformity arises from social influence, source monitoring errors, and narrative integration. Demonstrating susceptibility to one type of memory error does not validly demonstrate susceptibility to the other, and participants could reasonably reject the implied generalization. This undermines the construct validity of the demonstration manipulation.
issues.quote: 'First, in order to demonstrate to participants that they are vulnerable to influence, a substantially shortened and simplified procedure based on the DRM paradigm will be used...The results will be fed back to participants in order to demonstrate to them that their memory was vulnerable to a subtle influence.'

issues.description: The entire validity of the MORI paradigm rests on participants believing they watched the same movie as their partner. If a participant notices inconsistencies attributable to different movie versions (e.g., noticing the partner's answer is implausible given what they saw and inferring a different movie was shown), the experimental logic fails. The manuscript includes no protocol for checking whether participants suspected the dual-movie manipulation, no criteria for excluding such participants, and no procedure for probing this at debriefing in a way that would allow retrospective exclusion. The 'purpose of the study' open-ended question at debriefing is mentioned only for 'exploratory analysis of any relationship between hypothesis awareness and performance,' not for checking the core MORI manipulation validity.
issues.quote: 'Next, the subjects will be requested to say what they think the real purpose of the study was. Their responses will be recorded for exploratory analysis of any relationship between hypothesis awareness and performance.'

issues.subcategory: no blind scoring of open-ended responses
issues.description: The individual memory test uses open-ended questions. Scoring whether an answer is correct, consistent with misinformation, or falls into the 'other' category requires human judgment. No procedure for blind scoring—where scorers are unaware of participants' group assignment—is described. Experimenter expectancy effects in scoring open-ended memory data are well-documented and could systematically bias results in the direction of hypotheses, particularly for ambiguous responses. This is a standard requirement for studies using subjective scoring of open-ended responses and its absence is a significant methodological gap.
issues.quote: 'Four indices will be derived from the open-ended test: the number of: (1) correct answers (consistent with the movie), (2) answers consistent with the misinformation, (3) other answers (consistent neither with the movie nor the misinformation), and (4) the overall number of answers.'

issues.description: The Extended Warning reveals the deception: it informs participants that the partner saw a different movie version and explains why the deception was applied. When administered after collaborative recall but before the individual memory test, this enlightenment creates strong demand characteristics. Participants who now know there was a different movie version and that they may have given misinformation-consistent answers during discussion may try to 'correct' their answers on the individual test to appear more accurate—not because they genuinely remember the original information better, but because they are attempting to respond as the experimenter presumably wants. This would produce apparent intervention success that reflects social desirability rather than any genuine memory process, making it impossible to distinguish true reduction in memory conformity from strategic responding.
issues.quote: 'Extended warning, informing that the partner actually saw a different version of the movie and informing why the deception was applied, should make the participants who are aware of discrepancies discard the consistency assumption and make them rely on their own correct memories.'

issues.description: Four indices are derived from the individual memory test and all are listed as outcomes to be explored using ANOVA: (1) correct answers, (2) misinformation-consistent answers, (3) other answers, and (4) overall number of answers. No single primary outcome is designated, and no correction for multiple comparisons across these four correlated outcomes is discussed. Additionally, the analysis plan mentions observing 'individual memory test's average accuracy on the filler, non-discussed, and discussed questions,' adding further outcomes. Running multiple ANOVAs on correlated outcomes without a pre-specified primary endpoint and without familywise error correction substantially inflates Type I error. If only a subset of outcomes reaches significance, post-hoc designation of that outcome as primary would constitute a reporting bias.
issues.quote: 'We will explore the individual memory test's scores for the critical details using analysis of variance (ANOVA), using all four indices: the number of correct answers, number of answers consistent with misinformation, other answers, and the overall number of answers.'

issues.description: The only pre-specified exclusion criterion is 'any technical problems during the experimental session.' This is inadequate for a study involving interpersonal interaction, a deception paradigm, and multiple complex manipulations. Missing are criteria for: participants who become suspicious about seeing different movies; participants who already know each other (familiarity affects conformity; Condon et al., 2015, is even cited); participants who are not fluent in Polish; participants who fail attention checks; situations where one pair member drops out mid-session; non-compliance with the polarized glasses instruction; and cases where the collaborative recall discussion does not actually involve the critical details (e.g., agreement without genuine discussion). The vagueness of exclusion criteria creates post-hoc researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: '3.1. Exclusions: We will exclude participants in the case of any technical problems during the experimental session.'

issues.description: The design section states that 'pairs of participants will be randomly assigned to one of four groups,' which is methodologically appropriate given that pairs must interact together. However, the procedure section states that 'the participants will be randomly divided into four groups.' If pairs are split across conditions, members of the same pair could receive different interventions and potentially discuss or compare their experiences, causing contamination between conditions. The ambiguity about the unit of randomization—individual or pair—is consequential for both contamination risk and statistical analysis (it affects what the appropriate unit of analysis is).
issues.quote: Design section: 'Pairs of participants will be randomly assigned to one of four groups.' Procedure section: 'The participants will be randomly divided into four groups: in each of the first three, a different method of minimizing memory conformity will be applied.'

issues.subcategory: power analysis based on unstable joint effect size estimate
issues.description: The power analysis for detecting memory conformity combines two effect sizes (Hedges' g = 1.92, N = 55, and g = 0.38, N = 74) that differ by more than a factor of five. The authors acknowledge this as a 'rather large difference' and use random effects, yielding a joint estimate of g = 1.13. However, with only two studies and such extreme heterogeneity, the random effects estimate is highly unstable with very wide confidence intervals; the true effect in the current population could plausibly range from near-zero to very large. The resulting claim that a sample of 18 provides 90% power, and that 240 participants will be 'sufficient,' rests on an unreliable point estimate. Furthermore, the inter-item correlation of r = 0.07 used in the power analysis is near zero, which means the repeated-measures design provides almost no advantage over a between-subjects design, yet the minimum required N of 18 is presented without discussion of how sensitive this estimate is to the correlation assumption.
issues.quote: 'The existing results as regards effect sizes are Hedges' g = 1.92, N = 55 (Ito et al., 2019) and Hedges' g = 0.38, N = 74 (Kękuś et al., 2020). Given the rather large difference in effect sizes between both studies, random effects were assumed while calculating the joint effect size, which was 1.13...Under such conditions, the sample size required for 90% power was 18.'

issues.description: The control condition consists of a podcast on 'soft skills related to social attitudes.' This is problematic in several ways. First, the duration is unspecified, so it cannot be confirmed that the control condition is time-matched to the experimental conditions. Second, 'soft skills related to social attitudes' is a substantively loaded topic that could affect social cognition, interpersonal trust, or communication style, which could interact with the memory conformity process in unpredictable ways. A true attentional control—matched in duration, modality (podcast), and cognitive demand, but containing content entirely unrelated to memory, testimony, or social influence—would be needed to attribute group differences specifically to the intervention content rather than to generic effects of receiving relevant information.
issues.quote: 'In the control group, participants will listen to a podcast concerning soft skills related to social attitudes.' / '2.4.5. Materials for the control condition: In the control group, participants will listen to a podcast concerning soft skills related to social attitudes.'

issues.description: The study requires pairs of participants to attend together. No protocol is described for handling the situation where one member of a pair cancels, drops out mid-session, or must be excluded (e.g., due to technical failure with their polarized glasses). Given the logistical complexity of recruiting paired participants, this is a predictable and consequential source of data loss. If one member is excluded, should the remaining participant's data be retained as a single-person observation (which would be conceptually inconsistent with the paired design and the social nature of the misinformation), discarded entirely (losing data), or replaced? The absence of this protocol introduces potential post-hoc decision-making that could bias results.
issues.quote: 'The sample size will be set at 240 people (120 pairs).' [No attrition protocol is described anywhere in the manuscript.]

issues.description: The sample is restricted to 16–35 year olds, recruited via media and internet advertisements in Poland. The age restriction is justified only in terms of preventing confounding from age-discrepant pairs, but the broader restriction to young adults is not discussed as a limitation on generalizability. Memory conformity processes may differ substantially in older adults, children, or populations with different educational or cultural backgrounds. The recruitment method (internet and media advertisements in one country) produces a self-selected sample with potentially atypical characteristics (e.g., curiosity-seekers, those comfortable with psychological research). These limitations are not acknowledged in the manuscript and no discussion section addresses the boundary conditions of the findings.
issues.quote: 'The participants enrolled in the study will be 16–35 years old; they will be invited to participate via advertisements in the media and on the internet. The age of the participants will be restricted in order to avoid a situation in which a very young participant would discuss the original material with an elderly one, which would possibly activate some confounding factors.'

issues.subcategory: IMP framework transferred without sufficient justification
issues.description: The Integrative Framework for Memory and Performance (IMP; Blank, 1998) serves as the primary theoretical foundation for all three interventions. However, the IMP was explicitly developed for the classic misinformation paradigm where post-event information is delivered impersonally (e.g., via a written narrative). The authors acknowledge this: 'The IMP was developed in the context of the classic misinformation paradigm...However, similar processes may apply to the memory conformity paradigm.' This 'may apply' is the sole justification for a theoretical transfer between paradigms that differ in social dynamics (interpersonal vs. impersonal source), misinformation delivery (oral discussion vs. written text), source credibility (known peer vs. anonymous experimenter-provided text), and the consistency assumption dynamics. Memory conformity involves real-time negotiation and social identity concerns that are absent from impersonal misinformation delivery. The theoretical transfer requires more rigorous justification.
issues.quote: 'The IMP was developed in the context of the classic misinformation paradigm, in which the post-event information is delivered impersonally. However, similar processes may apply to the memory conformity paradigm.'

issues.description: The authors predict that Demonstration and motivation will be most effective, Extended warning second, and Education about memory least effective. The rationale for the intermediate ranking of Extended warning above Education about memory is weak because Extended warning explicitly includes many of the same components as Education about memory (information about memory fallibility, the misinformation effect, source misattribution, examples). The theoretical difference between presenting memory failure information as a 'warning' versus 'education' is not clearly operationalized. If Extended warning and Education about memory produce similar outcomes, it cannot distinguish between the interventions being equally effective versus the theoretical distinctions being empirically inoperative. The authors acknowledge 'some overlap between the three interventions' but do not address how this undermines the ordered predictions.
issues.quote: 'Moreover, on the basis of the fact that warning in general has produced inconsistent results in the context of undoing various kinds of suggestive influence, the Extended warning against misinformation is expected to be slightly less effective than Demonstration and motivation but more effective than Education about memory. We hypothesize so because Education about memory only consists in providing theoretical knowledge but does not demonstrate any effects or motivate participants.'

issues.subcategory: no ethics approval or pre-registration statement
issues.description: The manuscript contains no statement of ethics board approval or exemption, no participant informed consent protocol, no description of how participants are debriefed about the deception (only a brief mention that 'the participants will be debriefed'), and no pre-registration identifier. Despite the paper appearing to be a registered report (referencing 'Stage 1 review'), there is no registration number, registry name, or link provided. Given that the study involves active deception of participants and the use of DRM feedback that tells participants their memory was 'fooled,' the absence of ethics and deception-handling details is a notable reporting gap.
issues.quote: 'Finally, the participants will be debriefed. One experimental session will last about 60 minutes.' / '3.2. Timeline for completion of the study: If the Stage 1 review is accepted, the resubmission should be completed no later than in 2023.'
